P2Q1.q: According to Aquinas, what makes an action properly "human" rather than merely "an action of a man"?
options: That it produces a visible external effect
That it proceeds from a deliberate will, i.e. from reason and free-will
That it is performed in public
That it is habitual and repeated often
P2Q1.explanation: Aquinas says only actions of which man is master, proceeding from a deliberate will (reason and will), are properly called "human"; other actions are merely "of a man."

P2Q1.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that there must be one last end of human life (Article 4)?
options: Because Scripture names only one end explicitly
Because an infinite regress in the order of ends is impossible; without a last end nothing would be desired and the appetite would never rest
Because philosophers before him agreed on a single end
Because human life has a fixed biological limit
P2Q1.explanation: Just as there cannot be an infinite regress of movers, there cannot be an infinite series of ends; if there were no last end, nothing would be desired and the intention of the agent would never come to rest.

P2Q1.q: In Article 7, in what sense does Aquinas say all men have the same last end?
options: All men agree only in the general notion of a fulfilling, perfect good, though they disagree about the concrete thing in which it consists
All men consciously seek God as their last end
All men pursue wealth as their practical last end
All men have identical last ends because society determines individual desires
P2Q1.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the formal aspect of "last end" (which all desire, namely fulfillment) from the concrete thing that realizes it (riches, pleasure, etc.), on which men disagree.

P2Q2.q: Why, according to Article 1, can man's happiness not consist in wealth?
options: Because wealth is evil in itself
Because wealth (natural or artificial) is sought only as useful for something else, not as an end in itself
Because the poor cannot be happy
Because wealth cannot be possessed permanently
P2Q2.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes natural wealth (a remedy for natural wants) from artificial wealth (money, invented for exchange); both are ordered to something further, so neither can be the last end.

P2Q2.q: Why can happiness not consist in power, according to Article 4?
options: Because power is always abused
Because power has the nature of a principle (ordained to something further) whereas happiness has the nature of a last end, and power relates indifferently to good and evil
Because only kings possess power
Because power diminishes over time
P2Q2.explanation: Aquinas gives two reasons: power is a principle for acting, not a final end, and since power can be used well or badly it cannot itself be man's perfect good.

P2Q2.q: According to Article 8, why must happiness ultimately be found in God rather than any created good?
options: Because creation is inherently corrupt
Because the will's object is the universal good, and only God possesses goodness essentially rather than by participation
Because only God can be perceived by the senses
Because created goods are always temporary
P2Q2.explanation: Since the will's object is universal good and every creature has goodness only by participation, only God, who is goodness itself, can satisfy the will completely.

P2Q3.q: In Article 2, what does Aquinas conclude that happiness, considered as something created and existing in man, essentially is?
options: A habit acquired through virtue
An operation, since happiness is man's supreme perfection and each thing is perfect insofar as it is in act
A feeling of pleasure
A possession of external goods
P2Q3.explanation: Aquinas argues that since potentiality without act is imperfect, and operation is the "last act" of a power, man's happiness must consist in an operation.

P2Q3.q: According to Article 5, is perfect happiness an operation of the practical or the speculative intellect?
options: The practical intellect, since happiness concerns action
Neither, since happiness is purely an act of will
The speculative intellect, since man's highest power's highest object (the Divine Good) belongs to contemplation, not to practical action
Both equally, in balanced measure
P2Q3.explanation: Aquinas reasons that happiness must be man's highest operation, and man's highest power (intellect) attains its highest object (the Divine Good) through contemplation, i.e., the speculative intellect.

P2Q3.q: What does Aquinas conclude, in Article 8, is the only thing in which final and perfect happiness can consist?
options: Knowledge of separate substances such as angels
Moral virtue perfected over a lifetime
The vision of the Divine Essence
Mastery of the speculative sciences
P2Q3.explanation: Because man is not perfectly happy while something remains to be known, and the intellect's perfection lies in knowing a cause's essence, final happiness must be the direct vision of God's Essence.

P2Q4.q: According to Article 3, what three things does Aquinas say must concur in perfect Happiness?
options: Wealth, honor, and fame
Vision (perfect knowledge of the end), comprehension (presence of the end), and delight/enjoyment (rest of the lover in the object)
Faith, hope, and charity alone
Health of body, wealth, and friendship
P2Q4.explanation: Corresponding to man's threefold ordering to an end through intellect and will, perfect Happiness requires vision, comprehension, and delight.

P2Q4.q: Regarding the body and happiness in Article 5, what does Aquinas conclude?
options: The body is absolutely required even for perfect happiness in the vision of God
The body is required for the imperfect happiness of this life (which needs phantasms), but not for the perfect happiness of the separated soul's vision of God
Happiness is impossible without perfect bodily health
The soul cannot function at all apart from the body
P2Q4.explanation: Aquinas holds that intellectual operation in this life needs phantasms rooted in bodily organs, but the separated souls of the saints already "walk by sight," seeing God's Essence without their bodies.

P2Q4.q: Why, according to Article 8, does the happy man need the fellowship of friends in this life?
options: Because he cannot be happy without being used and served by others
Not to use them or to find delight in them, since he suffices himself, but for the purpose of good operation—to do good to them and be helped by them in good works
Because friendship is required to attain the vision of God
Because without friends a man cannot acquire wealth
P2Q4.explanation: Aquinas, following Aristotle, says the happy man needs friends for the sake of good action—doing good to them, delighting in their good deeds, and being helped in his own.

P2Q5.q: According to Article 5, can man attain perfect happiness by his own natural powers alone?
options: Yes, through sufficient effort and virtue
No, because the vision of God's Essence surpasses the nature of every creature, not only man's
Yes, but only for exceptionally wise philosophers
No, because happiness is entirely a matter of chance
P2Q5.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the vision of the Divine Essence infinitely surpasses all created substance, neither man nor any creature can attain final Happiness by natural powers.

P2Q5.q: According to Article 4, can the imperfect happiness available in this life be lost?
options: No, once attained it is permanent
Yes—for example, contemplative happiness can be lost through sickness or through being drawn away by other occupations
Only through death
No, because true happiness by definition cannot be lost
P2Q5.explanation: Aquinas states that imperfect happiness in this life, such as contemplative happiness, can be lost through forgetfulness (e.g., illness) or through preoccupations that withdraw a man from contemplation.

P2Q5.q: In Article 8, why does Aquinas say every man desires happiness, even though not everyone agrees on what happiness is?
options: Because everyone has been taught the same definition of happiness
Because, under the general notion of the perfect good that satisfies the will, all necessarily desire happiness, even though they differ about the specific thing in which it consists
Because desire for happiness is a cultural convention
Because all men desire wealth above all else
P2Q5.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the general notion of happiness (the perfect good that satisfies the will, which all desire of necessity) from its specific notion (the particular thing that is happiness), about which people disagree.

P2Q6.q: According to Article 1, what two things are essential to a voluntary act?
options: Physical strength and social approval
An intrinsic principle of the act together with some knowledge of the end
Divine command and human obedience
Habit and repetition
P2Q6.explanation: Aquinas holds that a voluntary act requires that its principle be within the agent, together with some knowledge of the end for which it acts.

P2Q6.q: How does Aquinas classify actions done through fear in Article 6?
options: Simply voluntary, since fear does not affect the will
Simply involuntary, since fear compels the will entirely
Mixed—involuntary considered in itself, but voluntary in the particular circumstance, since it is chosen to avoid a still-worse evil
Neither voluntary nor involuntary, but morally neutral
P2Q6.explanation: Following Aristotle, Aquinas says actions done through fear are "of a mixed character": not voluntary considered absolutely, but voluntary in the particular case as a means of avoiding the feared evil.

P2Q6.q: Does concupiscence (desire) cause involuntariness, according to Article 7?
options: Yes, because desire overrides free choice
No—on the contrary, concupiscence makes an act voluntary, since it inclines the will toward the desired object
Yes, but only in the case of extreme passion
It has no effect on voluntariness either way
P2Q6.explanation: Aquinas argues that concupiscence inclines the will to desire its object, so its effect is to make an act more voluntary rather than involuntary.

P2Q7.q: According to Article 2, why must theologians take note of the circumstances of human acts?
options: Only because circumstances make stories more interesting

Because acts must be proportionate to happiness as their end, because moral goodness or evil depends on circumstances, and because merit or demerit requires voluntariness, which depends on knowledge of circumstances
Because circumstances have no real bearing on morality
Because civil law requires it
P2Q7.explanation: Aquinas gives a threefold reason: circumstances affect an act's proportion to its end, its degree of goodness or evil, and whether it is voluntary (hence meritorious or blameworthy).

P2Q7.q: Which two circumstances does Aquinas identify in Article 4 as the most important?
options: Where and when the act occurred
Who did it and by what means
"Why" (the end) and "what he did" (the substance of the act)
How much and how often
P2Q7.explanation: Since acts are human insofar as voluntary, and the will's object is the end, the circumstance of "why" is most important, followed by the circumstance touching the very substance of the act.

P2Q7.q: According to Article 1, from what domain is the word "circumstance" metaphorically borrowed to describe features of human acts?
options: From medicine and the treatment of illness
From local, spatial position—things that "stand around" a located thing
From military strategy
From commerce and exchange
P2Q7.explanation: Aquinas explains that just as intellectual knowledge proceeds from what is better known (bodies located in place) to what is less obvious, the term "circumstance," originally spatial, was transferred to describe the accidental conditions of acts.

P2Q8.q: According to Article 1, what alone is the object of the will?
options: The pleasant
The good, since the will is a rational appetite and every appetite tends only to something good
Whatever the intellect commands regardless of goodness
Being in general, whether good or evil
P2Q8.explanation: Aquinas states the will is a rational appetite, and every appetite is only of something good, since every inclination is toward something suitable, i.e. good.

P2Q8.q: In Article 2, does volition concern only the last end, or also the means?
options: Only the last end
Both the end and the means, since the will as a power extends to anything in which the aspect of good can be found
Only the means, never the end itself
Neither; volition only concerns feelings
P2Q8.explanation: Aquinas explains that the will as a power extends to both end and means because the aspect of good, its object, is found in both.

P2Q8.q: According to Article 3, how does the will's movement toward the end relate to its movement toward the means?
options: They are always entirely separate and unrelated acts
The will can be moved to the end without being moved to the means, but is moved to the means (as such) only by the same movement by which it is moved to the end as the reason for willing them
The will is moved to the means first, and only afterward to the end
The end and means are always willed simultaneously by identical, indistinguishable acts in every case
P2Q8.explanation: Aquinas holds that willing the means presupposes willing the end as the reason for the means (one movement), while the will can also be moved to the end absolutely in itself by a distinct act, which can precede in time.

P2Q9.q: According to Article 1, how does the intellect move the will?
options: By physically forcing it to act
By presenting the good as an object, since a power in potentiality to several things needs to be moved by something actual, in this case as to specification of the act
The intellect has no influence over the will at all
By replacing the will's function entirely
P2Q9.explanation: Aquinas explains the will, like other powers, is in potentiality to different acts and objects, and the intellect moves it by presenting the object (the apprehended good) that specifies its act.

P2Q9.q: According to Article 3, can the will move itself?
options: No, the will can only be moved by external causes
Yes, through willing the end, the will moves itself to will the means, just as the intellect through principles moves itself to conclusions
No, self-motion is logically impossible for any power
Yes, but only in irrational creatures
P2Q9.explanation: Aquinas draws an analogy: just as the intellect, through knowledge of a principle, reduces itself to actually knowing a conclusion, the will, through willing the end, moves itself to will the means.

P2Q9.q: According to Article 6, who alone can move the will as an exterior principle with respect to the interior act of willing itself?
options: Any powerful human authority
The heavenly bodies
God alone, since only the cause of the will's very nature can move it in the manner natural to it
Angels acting on their own authority
P2Q9.explanation: Aquinas reasons that just as only the cause of a stone's nature can cause its natural downward movement, only God, as cause of the will's nature, can be the will's exterior mover in the proper, interior sense.

P2Q10.q: According to Article 2, under what condition does an object move the will of necessity?
options: Whenever the object is presented clearly to the senses
Only when the object is good in every respect and lacking in nothing—i.e., perfect Happiness—since particular goods, being deficient in some respect, do not move the will of necessity
Whenever the object is commanded by legitimate authority
Never; the will is always moved with absolute necessity by any object
P2Q10.explanation: Aquinas compares this to sight and color: an object that is good from every point of view (Happiness) moves the will necessarily, but a good lacking in some respect (a particular good) does not.

P2Q10.q: According to Article 3, can passion of the sensitive appetite ever remove the free use of reason and will entirely?
options: No, passion can never affect reason or will at all
Yes—when passion is so violent that reason is wholly bound (as in fury or insanity), a person then acts of necessity, like irrational animals
Only in animals, never in human beings
Yes, but only regarding purely intellectual judgments, never regarding action
P2Q10.explanation: Aquinas acknowledges that in cases of violent passion that entirely bind the use of reason, the will follows the passion of necessity, comparable to how irrational animals follow their impulses.

P2Q10.q: According to Article 4, does God's moving of the will destroy its freedom or contingency?
options: Yes, God's causality makes every act of will strictly necessary
No; Divine providence moves each thing according to its own nature, so it moves the will as a contingent cause, preserving its freedom except toward what it wills naturally
God does not move the will at all, leaving it entirely autonomous
Yes, but only for sinners, while the righteous retain freedom
P2Q10.explanation: Citing Dionysius, Aquinas holds that Providence preserves the nature of things it moves; since the will is a contingent, non-determined power, God moves it contingently, not of necessity, except with respect to things willed naturally (like Happiness in general).

P2Q11.q: According to Article 1, to what power does "fruition" (enjoyment) belong?
options: The apprehensive power, since it requires knowledge
The appetitive power, since fruition denotes delight in realizing the longed-for term, i.e. the end
The nutritive power, since it derives from sensible fruit
The imaginative power alone
P2Q11.explanation: Aquinas connects fruition to delight in attaining what is longed for, and since the end and the good are objects of the appetitive power, fruition is an act of that power.

P2Q11.q: According to Article 2, do irrational animals enjoy their ends?
options: Yes, in exactly the same way as rational creatures
No, strictly speaking, because enjoyment belongs to the power that commands the end, not merely the power that executes it, and irrational things lack that commanding power in themselves
Yes, because all animals seek pleasure
No animal, rational or not, can properly be said to enjoy anything
P2Q11.explanation: Aquinas argues that irrational things attain an end through natural tendency but do not have within themselves a governing appetite ordered by reason, so, strictly, only creatures endowed with knowledge and command over their appetite can enjoy an end.

P2Q11.q: According to Article 3, of what is enjoyment properly said to be?
options: Any pleasurable experience whatsoever
Only the last end, in which the will finds absolute rest, not something desired merely as a means to something else
Only bodily pleasures
Any intermediate goal along the way
P2Q11.explanation: Aquinas explains that "fruit" implies something ultimate that calms the appetite with delight; what is desired only for the sake of something else (like a bitter medicine for health) is not properly enjoyed.

P2Q12.q: According to Article 1, to which faculty does "intention" properly belong?
options: The intellect, since it involves understanding
The will, since intention belongs to that which moves toward an end, and the will moves the other powers of the soul to the end
The imagination
The sensitive appetite exclusively
P2Q12.explanation: Aquinas explains intention means "to tend to something," which belongs to the mover; since the will moves all other powers toward the end, intention is properly an act of the will.

P2Q12.q: According to Article 2, is intention always of the very last end?
options: Yes, intention can never regard an intermediate goal
No; intention can regard an intermediate terminus (like a midway point B on the way to C) as well as the ultimate terminus
Intention only ever concerns means, never ends
Intention and choice are identical acts with identical objects
P2Q12.explanation: Aquinas compares intention to a terminus of movement, which can be either the final terminus or a midpoint that is both a beginning and an end of part of the movement; thus intention need not always be of the absolutely last end.

P2Q12.q: According to Article 3, can a person intend two things at the same time?
options: Never under any circumstances
Yes, if the two things are ordained to one another, such as a proximate end (mixing a medicine) and the further end it serves (giving health)
Yes, but only if the two things are completely unrelated
No, human intention is always confined to a single indivisible object
P2Q12.explanation: Aquinas holds that when things are ordained to one another, a person can intend both the proximate and the ultimate end simultaneously, as in mixing a medicine for the sake of health.

P2Q13.q: According to Article 1, what does choice involve, combining which two elements?
options: Pure appetite alone, with no role for reason
Something belonging to reason (counsel) and something belonging to the will (appetite)—an intellect influenced by appetite, or appetite influenced by intellect
Pure intellect alone, with no involvement of the will
Random impulse unconnected to either faculty
P2Q13.explanation: Citing Aristotle, Aquinas describes choice as a combination of desire and counsel, comparable to how an animal is composed of both soul and body.

P2Q13.q: According to Article 3, is choice ever of the last end, or only of the means?
options: Choice is always of the last end, never of means
Choice is properly only of the means, since in practical matters the end functions as a principle (presupposed), not as a conclusion to be chosen
Choice concerns neither ends nor means, only feelings
Choice and intention are identical in every respect
P2Q13.explanation: Aquinas explains that choice follows from a practical syllogism's conclusion, and since the end functions as a principle rather than a conclusion in practical reasoning, the end as such is not an object of choice.

P2Q13.q: According to Article 6, does man choose of necessity or freely?
options: Man chooses of necessity, since reason always dictates one determinate option

Man chooses freely, because reason can apprehend both the good and the corresponding lack of good in particular goods, so it can regard any of them as either to be chosen or avoided (unlike Happiness itself, which is willed of necessity)
Man never truly chooses; all human action is instinctual
Choice is entirely random and has no connection to reason
P2Q13.explanation: Aquinas argues that while man wills Happiness (the perfect good) of necessity, choice concerns particular goods, in which reason can always see some lacking aspect, so man is not determined to choose any one of them—hence choice is free.

P2Q14.q: According to Article 1, why is counsel described as an "inquiry"?
options: Because it is a formal legal proceeding
Because actions concern contingent, uncertain singulars, so reason must investigate before judging what is to be chosen
Because it always involves consulting written texts
Because it is identical with prayer
P2Q14.explanation: Since actions deal with contingent particulars that admit of uncertainty, reason cannot judge without prior inquiry, and this inquiry is called counsel.

P2Q14.q: According to Article 2, is counsel about the end or about the means?
options: Counsel is about the end alone, since ends are always uncertain
Properly, counsel is not about the end (which is presupposed as a principle), but about the means, though what is an end in one context can be a means examined by counsel in another
Counsel concerns neither ends nor means, only past events
Counsel and choice are always about entirely different matters, with no overlap
P2Q14.explanation: Aquinas explains that the end functions as a principle in practical reasoning and cannot be called into question by the very inquiry it grounds, so, properly, counsel concerns the means; though a subordinate end can become an object of counsel relative to a further end.

P2Q14.q: According to Article 5, in what direction does the process of counsel proceed?
options: Synthetically, from cause to effect
Analytically, beginning from what is intended in the future (the end) and proceeding back to what is to be done at once
Randomly, with no order at all
Only backward through past experiences, never forward
P2Q14.explanation: Since the end, though first in intention, comes last in execution, the inquiry of counsel is one of analysis, tracing back from the intended end to the immediate action to be done.

P2Q15.q: According to Article 1, to what power does consent belong?
options: The apprehensive power, since it requires understanding of the situation
The appetitive power, since consent implies the appetite "cleaving to" or taking complacency in a thing, likened metaphorically to sense
The purely vegetative power
No power at all, since it is merely verbal
P2Q15.explanation: Aquinas explains that consent, though named by analogy to sense (direct cognizance), is really an act of the appetitive power applying itself to and taking complacency in an object.

P2Q15.q: According to Article 2, do irrational animals properly have consent?
options: Yes, fully and properly, since all animals have appetites
No, properly speaking, because consent requires having command over the appetitive movement, applying it to this or that object—something only rational creatures can do
Yes, but only in domesticated animals
Consent applies equally to plants and animals
P2Q15.explanation: Aquinas argues that irrational animals' appetitive movement follows natural instinct rather than being applied by their own command to a particular object, so consent, properly speaking, belongs to rational nature alone.

P2Q15.q: According to Article 3, to what is consent, properly speaking, directed?
options: Only to the last end itself
Only to the means, since consent is the application of the appetitive movement to the decision reached through counsel, and counsel is only about means
Equally and always to both end and means without distinction
To nothing in particular; consent is not directed to any object
P2Q15.explanation: Since the appetite tends to the last end naturally (simple volition) and counsel concerns only the means, consent as application of appetite to counsel's decision is, properly speaking, only of the means.

P2Q16.q: According to Article 1, to what power does "use" of a thing properly belong?
options: The reason alone, as director
The will, as the power that first applies other powers and things to an operation, though reason directs and other powers execute
The external members of the body exclusively
The imagination, since use requires picturing an action beforehand
P2Q16.explanation: Aquinas explains that use is the application of something to an operation; since it is the will that moves the soul's powers to their acts (applying them to operation), use belongs first and principally to the will.

P2Q16.q: According to Article 3, does "use" ever regard the last end itself?
options: Yes, use always and primarily regards the last end
No; since use implies applying one thing to another as a means, use always regards the means, not the last end
Use regards only bodily pleasures
Use and enjoyment (fruition) are identical acts with identical objects
P2Q16.explanation: Because use implies applying something to another as to an end (i.e., as a means), it always regards the means and not the last end, which is why useful things are called "useful."

P2Q16.q: According to Article 2, is "use" found in irrational animals?
options: Yes, since animals clearly use tools like sticks and stones
No, because only a rational agent, capable of referring one thing to another (an act of reason), can properly be said to use and to consent
Yes, but only in animals trained by humans
Use is found in plants but not animals
P2Q16.explanation: Aquinas argues that referring something to an end requires an act of reason, which is why only a rational animal, not an irrational one, properly consents and uses.

P2Q17.q: According to Article 1, is command an act of the reason or of the will?
options: Purely an act of the will with no involvement of reason
An act of the reason, but one that presupposes an act of the will, since reason and will's acts bear upon one another
Purely an act of the sensitive appetite
An act belonging to neither reason nor will, but to memory alone
P2Q17.explanation: Aquinas explains that command is an act of reason directing something toward an end, but this directing act presupposes that the will has already willed that end, so the two acts are intertwined.

P2Q17.q: According to Article 7, is the act of the sensitive appetite subject to the command of reason?
options: Not at all, since the sensitive appetite is entirely independent of reason

Yes, but only indirectly and imperfectly, since the sensitive appetite depends not only on the appetitive power but also on the disposition of a bodily organ, which is not wholly under reason's control
Yes, completely and without qualification, exactly like the intellect's own acts
No, because the sensitive appetite does not exist in human beings
P2Q17.explanation: Aquinas notes the sensitive appetite is a power of a bodily organ, so its acts depend partly on the condition of that organ; hence it is subject to reason's command only to the extent that reason can influence that bodily disposition.

P2Q17.q: According to Article 8, are the acts of the vegetal soul (such as nutrition and generation) subject to command of reason?
options: Yes, fully, since reason governs the entire soul
No, because these acts proceed from natural appetite, which does not follow from any apprehension, whereas reason commands only what proceeds from apprehensive/appetitive powers
Yes, but only during sleep
No acts of the soul are ever subject to reason's command
P2Q17.explanation: Since reason commands by way of the apprehensive power, and the natural appetite (governing vegetal functions like nutrition and generation) does not arise from apprehension, such acts are not subject to reason's command.

P2Q18.q: According to Article 2, from what does a human action primarily derive its species as good or evil?
options: From the intention of bystanders
From its object, just as a natural thing's species is derived from its form
From the time at which it occurs
From whether it succeeds or fails
P2Q18.explanation: Aquinas compares an action's object to a natural thing's form: just as form gives a natural thing its species, an action's suitable or unsuitable object gives it its primary moral goodness or evil "in its genus."

P2Q18.q: According to Article 4, does a human action's goodness or evil also depend on its end?
options: No, only the object matters, never the end
Yes; since the goodness of things whose being depends on something else is measured by that on which they depend, human actions (which depend on their end) are also judged by their end
No, the end is only relevant to non-human agents
Yes, but only for actions performed in public
P2Q18.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as a thing's being can depend on an external cause, human actions' goodness depends on their end besides whatever goodness they have absolutely considered in themselves.

P2Q18.q: According to Article 8, can any human action be indifferent (neither good nor evil) according to its species?
options: No, every action is necessarily either good or evil in species
Yes—for example, picking up a straw from the ground, an action whose object includes nothing that accords or conflicts with the order of reason
No, indifference is impossible because reason judges every conceivable object
Yes, and in fact most human actions are indifferent in species
P2Q18.explanation: Aquinas explains that when an action's object neither includes something in accord with reason's order nor something repugnant to it, the action is indifferent according to its species, giving the example of picking up a straw.

P2Q19.q: According to Article 3, on what does the goodness of the will depend, in addition to its object?
options: On reason, since the will's object (the good understood) is proposed to it by reason, unlike sensitive appetite which is proportioned to sensible good
On the color of objects perceived
On physical strength alone
On social consensus regarding what is good
P2Q19.explanation: Aquinas explains the will's proper object, the good as understood, is proposed to it by reason (unlike the sensitive appetite, proportioned to particular sensible goods), so the goodness of the will depends on reason as well as on the object.

P2Q19.q: According to Article 5, is the will evil whenever it disagrees with an erring reason or conscience?
options: Always evil in every case without exception
It depends on the matter: reason/conscience errs bindingly in matters of indifference, but there is more nuance when reason commands what is evil in itself or forbids what is necessary for salvation
Never evil, since conscience is always infallible
The question is irrelevant because reason never errs
P2Q19.explanation: Aquinas discusses the classic problem of whether an erring conscience binds, distinguishing cases of indifferent matters (where erring conscience does bind) from cases where conscience commands something evil in itself or forbids something necessary for salvation.

P2Q19.q: According to Article 9, on what does the ultimate goodness of the human will depend?
options: On its conformity to the Sovereign Good, God, since the goodness of the will depends on the intention of the end, and man's last end is God
On its conformity to popular opinion
On the amount of pleasure it produces
On its conformity strictly to civil law
P2Q19.explanation: Since the goodness of the will depends on the intention of the end (Article 7), and the last end of the human will is God as the Sovereign Good, the will's goodness ultimately requires being ordained to Him.

P2Q20.q: According to Article 1, where is goodness or malice found first: in the interior act of the will, or in the external action?
options: Always and only in the external action

In the act of the will first, considered as the external action's goodness in relation to its end, though goodness from due matter and circumstances comes from reason and, in execution, follows from the will
External actions have no moral quality whatsoever
Goodness is located equally and identically in both, with no priority
P2Q20.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes: goodness relative to the end is found first in the will (whence it passes to the external act), while goodness from due matter/circumstances comes from reason, though as executed it follows upon the will's goodness.

P2Q20.q: According to Article 4, does the external action ever add any goodness or malice beyond that of the interior act?
options: No, external action can never add anything to interior goodness or malice
Yes, it can, in three ways: by number (repeated willing), by extension/duration (persevering in the will), and by intensity (external acts making the will itself more intense)
Only by increasing the actor's reputation
Only in cases of accidental, unintended outcomes
P2Q20.explanation: Aquinas explains the external action can increase the goodness or malice of the will itself in point of number, duration, and intensity, even though its goodness in relation to the end comes wholly from the will.

P2Q20.q: According to Article 6, can one and the same external action be both morally good and morally evil at once?
options: Yes, always, since every action has both good and bad aspects simultaneously

No; if considered as one action in the moral order (unified by a single act of will), it cannot be both good and evil at once, though it could be one physically while being morally multiple if the will changes during it
Only for actions performed by more than one person
Moral goodness and evil are illusions with no real basis in actions
P2Q20.explanation: Aquinas argues that unity in the moral order depends on the unity of the will's act; one continuous physical action (like walking) can become morally multiple if the walker's will changes, but a single moral action cannot be simultaneously both good and evil.

P2Q21.q: According to Article 1, in what sense is a human action called "right" or "sinful"?
options: "Right" and "sinful" only apply to actions judged by civil courts
An action is right when it accords with the due order to its end (measured by a rule such as natural inclination or reason), and sinful when it strays from that rectitude
These terms are purely a matter of subjective preference
Sin refers to any evil whatsoever, with no distinct sense of its own
P2Q21.explanation: Aquinas explains that sin is more specific than mere evil: it concerns an action done for an end but lacking due order to that end, judged by a governing rule.

P2Q21.q: According to Article 2, when is a human action said to deserve praise or blame?
options: Whenever it produces good or bad consequences, regardless of the agent's control
When it is imputed to the agent, i.e., when it is in the agent's power/dominion through the will
Only when performed in front of witnesses
Never, since praise and blame are meaningless categories
P2Q21.explanation: Aquinas ties praiseworthiness and blameworthiness to imputability: an act is imputed to an agent when it is under the agent's power through the will.

P2Q21.q: According to Article 4, do human actions acquire merit or demerit before God?
options: No, God is indifferent to human actions
Yes, both because God is man's last end (owed honor through referring actions to Him) and because God, as ruler of the universe, awards retribution for what is done well or ill in the community
Only actions performed inside a church acquire merit or demerit
Merit and demerit apply only to actions affecting other people, never oneself
P2Q21.explanation: Aquinas argues human actions merit or demerit before God both as our last end (owed due honor) and because God governs the whole universe and rewards or punishes accordingly.

P2Q22.q: According to Article 1, in what sense, properly speaking, are passions found in the soul?
options: Only in the sense of pure reception with no loss involved, like understanding
Properly speaking, passion (with loss of something and bodily transmutation) is in the soul only accidentally, i.e. insofar as the composite of soul and body is affected
Passions belong exclusively to the intellect, never to appetite
The soul cannot be said to have passions in any sense
P2Q22.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes passion in its most proper sense (involving bodily transmutation and loss, e.g. sickness) from a broader sense (mere reception, e.g. understanding); properly speaking, passion belongs to the soul only through the body-soul composite.

P2Q22.q: According to Article 2, is passion found more properly in the appetitive or the apprehensive power?
options: The apprehensive power, since knowledge causes the greatest change
The appetitive power, since the soul is drawn toward things themselves through appetite, whereas the apprehensive power knows things only through an "intention" it holds within itself
Passion belongs equally and identically to both powers
Neither power can properly be said to have passions
P2Q22.explanation: Aquinas argues passion implies being drawn toward what belongs to the agent; since the appetitive power relates to things as they exist in themselves (unlike apprehension, which deals with intentions/likenesses), passion fits the appetitive power more properly.

P2Q22.q: According to Article 3, is passion more properly found in the sensitive appetite or the intellectual appetite (will)?
options: The intellectual appetite (will), since it is the higher faculty
The sensitive appetite, because passion properly requires bodily transmutation, and the sensitive appetite (unlike the will) operates through a bodily organ
Passion is found equally in both without distinction
Neither the sensitive appetite nor the will can have passions
P2Q22.explanation: Since proper passion involves bodily transmutation, and the sensitive appetite (unlike the intellectual appetite, which needs no bodily organ) operates through the body, passion belongs more properly to the sensitive appetite.

P2Q23.q: According to Article 1, do the passions of the irascible part differ in species from those of the concupiscible part?
options: No, they are identical since both arise from the same power
Yes, because different powers have different objects, and the passions of different powers are referred to different objects, causing a difference not merely of species but of genus
They differ only in intensity, not in kind
The irascible part does not actually exist as distinct from the concupiscible part
P2Q23.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since the irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers with distinct objects, their passions differ not merely specifically, like species within one genus, but as belonging to different genera.

P2Q23.q: According to Article 3, why does anger have no contrary passion?
options: Because anger is caused by a difficult evil already present, so there is no possibility of a corresponding movement of withdrawal from an absent evil
Because anger is identical to joy
Because all passions are contrary to one another equally
Because anger does not really exist as a distinct passion
P2Q23.explanation: Aquinas explains anger arises from a present, difficult evil, and can only result in either succumbing (sadness) or attacking (anger); since the evil is already present, there is no possible movement of "withdrawal" to serve as anger's contrary.

P2Q23.q: According to Article 2, on what is the contrariety of the irascible passions based?
options: On the contrariety of good and evil in the same way as the concupiscible passions
On contrariety of approach and withdrawal with respect to the same term, since passion is a kind of movement and this is one of the two kinds of contrariety found in changes and movements
On no basis at all, since the irascible passions cannot be compared to one another
On differences of bodily organ affected
P2Q23.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes contrariety according to approach/withdrawal from the same term (proper to changes like generation/corruption) from contrariety of opposite termini; the irascible passions' contrariety follows the former kind.

P2Q24.q: According to Article 1, can moral good and evil be found in the passions of the soul?
options: Never, because passions are purely irrational movements outside reason's scope
Yes, when the passions are considered as subject to the command of reason and will, since they can then be called voluntary and thus morally good or evil
Only in the case of extremely violent passions
Passions are morally neutral in every possible sense, always and everywhere
P2Q24.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes passions considered simply as movements of irrational appetite (morally neutral in themselves) from passions as subject to reason and will's command, in which case they can be morally good or evil.

P2Q24.q: According to Article 3, according to Aquinas's own view (as opposed to the Stoics), do moderate passions controlled by reason increase or decrease the goodness of a human act?
options: They always decrease it, since any passion is an imperfection
They can increase the perfection of moral good, since it belongs to the perfection of human good that passions be moderated and controlled by reason
Passions have absolutely no bearing on the goodness of an act
Only bodily passions matter; passions of the will are irrelevant
P2Q24.explanation: Unlike the Stoics who held all passion diminishes goodness, Aquinas argues that when passions are moderated by reason, their control belongs to the perfection of moral good, since good extends to more of what pertains to man.

P2Q24.q: According to Article 2, how does Aquinas assess the disagreement between Stoics and Peripatetics on whether passions are evil?
options: He sides entirely with the Stoics that all passion is evil

He says the disagreement is largely verbal: the Stoics used "passion" to mean only disordered movements exceeding reason, while the Peripatetics used it more broadly to include moderate, reason-governed movements
He rejects both positions as entirely mistaken
He says the question cannot be resolved and remains permanently open
P2Q24.explanation: Aquinas notes the Stoics did not distinguish sense from intellect, so what they called evil "passion" was really disordered movement exceeding reason, while the Peripatetics' "good" passions were moderate ones—so the dispute is largely terminological.

P2Q25.q: According to Article 4, which four passions does Aquinas identify as the principal passions, and how are they distinguished?
options: Love, hatred, desire, and aversion, distinguished by intensity
Joy, sadness, hope, and fear—joy and sadness relate to present good and evil, while hope and fear relate to future good and evil
Anger, fear, love, and joy, distinguished by which bodily organ they affect
Pride, envy, gluttony, and lust, distinguished by their moral gravity
P2Q25.explanation: Aquinas explains joy and sadness are principal because all other passions terminate in them, while hope and fear are principal with respect to movement toward future good or evil.

P2Q25.q: According to Article 2, which passion does Aquinas identify as first among the concupiscible passions?
options: Hatred, since evil must be recognized before good can be pursued
Love, since good naturally precedes evil (which is merely privation of good), so passions regarding good precede those regarding evil
Fear, since self-preservation is the most basic drive
Desire, prior to any apprehension of good or evil
P2Q25.explanation: Since evil is a privation of good, and good naturally precedes evil, Aquinas concludes love (whose object is good) precedes its contrary and other concupiscible passions.

P2Q25.q: According to Article 1, why do the irascible passions include nothing pertaining to repose?
options: Because the irascible faculty deals only with what is arduous or difficult, and once we rest in a thing, we no longer regard it as arduous
Because the irascible faculty does not actually exist in human beings
Because repose belongs exclusively to the intellect, not to appetite
Because the irascible passions occur only in dreams
P2Q25.explanation: Aquinas notes that the object of the irascible faculty is something arduous; once something is attained and rested in, it is no longer regarded under the aspect of the arduous, so repose belongs to the concupiscible passions (joy, sadness), not the irascible.

P2Q26.q: According to Article 4, how does Aquinas divide love?
options: Into love of self and love of others only
Into love of concupiscence (toward the good one wishes for someone, oneself or another) and love of friendship (toward the one for whom that good is wished)
Into natural love and supernatural love only, with no other distinctions
Into love of the body and love of the soul
P2Q26.explanation: Following the idea that "to love is to wish good to someone," Aquinas distinguishes love of concupiscence (toward the good wished) from love of friendship (toward the person to whom good is wished).

P2Q26.q: According to Article 2, is love a passion?
options: No, love is purely spiritual and never a passion
Yes, properly so called when in the concupiscible faculty, since love is the change wrought in the appetite by the object, from which desire and then joy follow
Love is identical with joy and has no distinct nature
Love cannot be classified at all since it defies analysis
P2Q26.explanation: Aquinas describes love as the first change the appetible object works in the appetite (a complacency), from which desire (movement toward the object) and joy (rest in it) follow; properly, as it occurs in the concupiscible faculty, it is a passion.

P2Q26.q: According to Article 1, from where does love originate according to the will (rational or intellectual appetite)?
options: From an apprehension existing in the subject of the appetite itself, following freely, unlike the merely natural appetite
From an external, entirely unconscious biological process
From apprehension in something outside the loving subject, as with natural appetite
Love in the will is identical to love in irrational animals
P2Q26.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes three kinds of appetite: natural (from apprehension in another), sensitive (from apprehension in the subject but by necessity), and the will's rational appetite (from apprehension in the subject, following freely).

P2Q27.q: According to Article 1, what is the proper cause of love?
options: Knowledge alone, independent of any object
The good, since love implies a certain connaturalness or complacency of the lover for the object loved, which is what makes that object a good to the lover
Physical proximity alone
Random chance, unrelated to any object's qualities
P2Q27.explanation: Since love's object is the good (that which is akin and suitable to the lover), Aquinas concludes good is love's proper cause.

P2Q27.q: According to Article 2, is knowledge a cause of love?
options: No, love can arise entirely without any apprehension of the object
Yes, because good can be the object of appetite only insofar as it is apprehended, so love requires some knowledge of the good that is loved
Knowledge actively prevents love from arising
Knowledge is only relevant to hatred, never to love
P2Q27.explanation: Aquinas argues good is not an object of appetite except as apprehended, so knowledge (of the beloved good) is necessarily a cause of love, since love can only be for what is known in some way.

P2Q27.q: According to Article 3, is likeness a cause of love?
options: No, likeness has nothing to do with the causes of love
Yes, properly speaking, whether the likeness is of shared actual quality or of potentiality resembling another's actuality
Only physical resemblance causes love, never any other kind of similarity
Likeness only ever causes hatred, through rivalry
P2Q27.explanation: Aquinas identifies two kinds of likeness that cause love: sharing an actual quality (e.g., two white things) and the likeness of potentiality to a corresponding actuality.

P2Q28.q: According to Article 1, what is one effect of love regarding union?
options: Love always causes physical separation between lover and beloved
Union, understood as real union (presence) and union of affection, arising from an apprehension of oneness between lover and beloved—whether through love of concupiscence or love of friendship
Love has no connection to union of any kind
Union occurs only in love of friendship, never in love of concupiscence
P2Q28.explanation: Aquinas explains both love of concupiscence (apprehending the desired thing as belonging to one's well-being) and love of friendship (willing good to another as to oneself) involve an apprehension of oneness, producing union of affection, and sometimes real union.

P2Q28.q: According to Article 3, what does Aquinas mean by "ecstasy" as an effect of love?
options: A purely physical fainting spell unrelated to love
Being placed outside oneself, whether in apprehension (raised to higher knowledge or debased) or in appetite (the appetitive power borne toward something else, going forth out of itself)
A technical term used only in mystical theology, never applicable to ordinary love
An effect found only in love of concupiscence, never love of friendship
P2Q28.explanation: Aquinas explains ecstasy, "being placed outside oneself," can occur through the apprehensive power (raised to higher knowledge or lowered into passion) or through the appetitive power being drawn out toward the beloved.

P2Q28.q: According to Article 5, when does love wound the lover?
options: Love always wounds the lover regardless of its object
When the appetite is adapted to a good that is not suitable to the lover (as with love of sin), whereas love of a truly suitable good (as love of God) perfects and betters him
Love never has any negative effect on the lover under any circumstance
Only love of friendship, never love of concupiscence, can wound
P2Q28.explanation: Aquinas argues that adaptation to something unsuitable hurts and worsens a thing, so while love of a suitable good (like God) perfects the lover, love of an unsuitable good (like sin) wounds him.

P2Q29.q: According to Article 2, which passion does Aquinas say is the cause of hatred?
options: Hatred arises spontaneously with no prior cause
Love, since we must first recognize what agrees with us before recognizing what disagrees, and nothing is hated except as contrary to some suitable thing that is loved
Fear alone causes all hatred
Hatred and love arise completely independently of one another
P2Q29.explanation: Aquinas argues love (agreement with a suitable thing) must be considered prior to hatred (disagreement), since something is hated only as being contrary to something loved—so every hatred is caused by some love.

P2Q29.q: According to Article 4, can a man, properly speaking, hate himself?
options: Yes, self-hatred is common and psychologically normal
No, properly speaking, because everything naturally desires good for itself, and to love oneself is simply to will good to oneself, which occurs of necessity
Yes, but only among the wicked
Self-hatred and self-love are simply identical states
P2Q29.explanation: Since to love someone means to will good to them, and everything naturally wills good to itself, Aquinas concludes it is, properly speaking, impossible for a man to hate himself.

P2Q29.q: According to Article 3, can hatred be stronger than love?
options: Yes, hatred is always the more powerful passion
No, absolutely speaking, since an effect cannot be stronger than its cause, and every hatred arises from some love as its cause
Hatred and love are always exactly equal in strength
The comparison is meaningless since hatred and love are unrelated
P2Q29.explanation: Since hatred is caused by love, and an effect cannot exceed its cause in strength, Aquinas concludes hatred cannot be stronger than love, absolutely speaking.

P2Q30.q: According to Article 1, to which appetite does concupiscence, properly speaking, belong?
options: The intellectual appetite (will) exclusively
The sensitive appetite, specifically the concupiscible faculty, since concupiscence is a craving for pleasure belonging to the composite of soul and body
Concupiscence belongs to no appetite at all, being purely bodily reflex
It belongs equally and identically to both intellectual and sensitive appetite
P2Q30.explanation: Since concupiscence craves the pleasure of the united soul and body (sensible pleasure), Aquinas concludes it properly belongs to the sensitive appetite's concupiscible faculty.

P2Q30.q: According to Article 3, how does Aquinas distinguish natural from non-natural concupiscence?
options: Natural concupiscence craves what is suitable to the animal's nature (like food or drink); non-natural concupiscence ("cupidity") arises from something apprehended as good and suitable, not from bodily need itself
There is no real distinction; all concupiscence is identical in kind
Natural concupiscence pertains only to plants, non-natural only to animals
Non-natural concupiscence refers to concupiscence experienced only in dreams
P2Q30.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes concupiscence for things naturally suited to the animal (food, drink) from concupiscence for things merely apprehended as suitable and pleasurable, which he calls "not natural" and more properly "cupidity."

P2Q30.q: According to Article 4, can natural concupiscence be actually infinite?
options: Yes, natural concupiscence has no limits whatsoever
No, natural concupiscence cannot be actually infinite because it is for what nature requires, which is always something finite and fixed, though it can recur successively
Yes, because nature itself is infinite
Natural concupiscence is infinite only in animals, never in humans
P2Q30.explanation: Aquinas argues natural concupiscence tends to a fixed, finite measure required by nature (e.g., a finite amount of food), though it can arise again and again successively as bodily goods are used up.

P2Q31.q: According to Article 4, in which appetite is joy found, as distinct from bodily delight?
options: Only in the sensitive appetite
In the intellectual appetite (the will), since when reason apprehends something, the will can also be moved, and delight following on such rational apprehension is called joy
Joy and bodily delight are simply identical terms for the same thing
In no appetite at all; joy is purely intellectual with no appetitive component
P2Q31.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes delight following the reason's apprehension (called joy, found in the will) from mere bodily delight of the sensitive appetite.

P2Q31.q: According to Article 5, are bodily and sensible pleasures greater than spiritual and intellectual pleasures?
options: Yes, always, since bodily pleasures are more immediate

No; Aquinas argues that the operations of the sensitive and intellectual soul are themselves goods known by sense and intellect, from which pleasure also arises, not merely from external objects, implying spiritual pleasures can surpass bodily ones
Bodily and spiritual pleasures cannot be compared at all
Pleasure is entirely illusory in both cases
P2Q31.explanation: Aquinas notes that the soul's own operations (understanding, willing) are themselves goods that generate pleasure beyond mere bodily objects, laying groundwork for holding intellectual pleasures superior.

P2Q31.q: According to Article 3, how does Aquinas distinguish delight from joy?
options: They are entirely identical terms with no distinction

Delight is broader, including both natural/bodily delights and rational delights, but "joy" specifically refers to delight that follows reason, which is why irrational animals are said to have delight but not joy
Joy refers only to bodily delight, while delight refers only to spiritual pleasure
Delight is experienced only by animals, joy only by humans
P2Q31.explanation: Aquinas explains some delights are natural (of the body) and some are rational (following reason); joy specifically denotes delight that follows reason, so irrational animals have delight but not joy.

P2Q32.q: According to Article 1, what is the proper cause of pleasure?
options: External wealth alone
Operation, since pleasure requires both attainment of a suitable good and knowledge of that attainment, and each of these is itself achieved through an operation
Sleep and physical rest exclusively
Nothing; pleasure has no identifiable cause
P2Q32.explanation: Since pleasure requires attaining a suitable good (achieved by operation) and knowing that attainment (itself an operation), Aquinas concludes every pleasure results from some operation.

P2Q32.q: According to Article 3, which is greater: the pleasure of sensation (a thing actually present), of hope, or of memory?
options: The pleasure of memory is greatest, since the past cannot be lost
They are all exactly equal in every case

Sensation's pleasure is greatest because it involves actual real conjunction with the object; hope is second because it involves potential conjunction; memory is third, involving only conjunction of apprehension
Hope is always greatest because anticipation exceeds actual enjoyment
P2Q32.explanation: Aquinas ranks pleasures by the degree of conjunction with the good: sensation (actual, real conjunction) is greatest, followed by hope (potential real conjunction), then memory (mere apprehension).

P2Q32.q: According to Article 4, can sadness ever be a cause of pleasure?
options: No, sadness and pleasure are entirely unrelated and mutually exclusive
Yes, both in itself (bringing to mind something loved) and in memory (recalling deliverance from past sorrow, which is pleasant because absence of evil seems good)
Sadness can cause pleasure only in mentally disturbed individuals
Sadness is identical to pleasure, just under a different name
P2Q32.explanation: Aquinas explains sadness can cause pleasure by recalling something loved (even if its absence saddens), and remembered sadness can please us through the pleasure of having been delivered from it.

P2Q33.q: According to Article 1, what does Aquinas mean by "expansion" as an effect of pleasure?
options: A literal physical growth of bodily organs

A metaphorical dimension describing how pleasure, through apprehension of a perfection attained and the appetite's resting in and embracing the pleasurable object, is said to "expand" the mind and affections
An economic term describing increased wealth
A term used only for describing joy in animals, not humans
P2Q33.explanation: Aquinas explains that "breadth"/expansion, properly a bodily dimension, is applied metaphorically to pleasure: the mind is "expanded" by perceiving a spiritual perfection, and the affections "expand" by resting in and embracing the pleasurable object.

P2Q33.q: According to Article 4, in what two ways does pleasure perfect operation?
options: Only by making the operation more difficult

As an end (a further good added to the operation, like the repose of appetite in a presupposed good) and as an (indirect) agent, since taking pleasure in an action makes one more eagerly and carefully intent on it
Pleasure never perfects operation; it always hinders it
Only by lengthening the duration of the operation
P2Q33.explanation: Following Aristotle, Aquinas explains pleasure perfects operation as an added end (a further good completing it) and indirectly as an agent, by making one more attentive and eager in the operation performed with pleasure.

P2Q33.q: According to Article 3, does pleasure always hinder the use of reason?
options: Yes, in every instance without exception
No; "appropriate" pleasures taken in the very act of reason (such as contemplating or reasoning) actually help the act of reason, since we attend more carefully to what pleases us
Pleasure and reason are entirely unrelated to one another
Pleasure always destroys reason permanently once experienced
P2Q33.explanation: Aquinas, citing Aristotle, distinguishes appropriate pleasures (taken in reason's own act, which increase attentiveness and thus help reason) from pleasures from other sources, which can impede activity.

P2Q34.q: According to Article 1, what mistake does Aquinas attribute to those (like some Stoics) who held that all pleasure is evil?
options: They correctly analyzed all forms of pleasure but drew the wrong conclusion

They considered only sensible and bodily pleasures, not discriminating between the intelligible and the sensible, and their own inconsistent practice (taking pleasure while teaching against it) undermined their teaching
They had never experienced any pleasure themselves
They confused pleasure with pain entirely
P2Q34.explanation: Aquinas argues these thinkers failed to distinguish intelligible/spiritual pleasure from sensible/bodily pleasure, and notes that since no one can live entirely without bodily pleasure, their example undercut their own teaching.

P2Q34.q: According to Article 2, what error does Aquinas attribute to the Epicureans, who held all pleasures are good?
options: They correctly identified that all pleasure is good simply, with no qualification needed
They failed to distinguish between what is good simply (in itself) and what is merely good relative to a particular individual's (sometimes unnatural) disposition
They denied that pleasure exists at all
They held that only intellectual pleasures are good, contrary to what Aquinas says they actually held
P2Q34.explanation: Aquinas explains the Epicureans erred by not distinguishing pleasure that is good simply (resting in a truly good object) from pleasure that is merely good relative to an individual's disordered disposition (like a leper enjoying poison).

P2Q34.q: According to Article 4, what does Aquinas say is the relationship between pleasure and moral judgment of a person's character?
options: Pleasure has no bearing whatsoever on moral character

Since moral goodness or evil depends chiefly on the will, and the will's repose in good is pleasure, a man is judged good or evil chiefly according to what gives him pleasure—the virtuous man delights in virtuous works, the evil man in evil works
Only external actions matter for moral judgment, never internal pleasure
Pleasure is always morally neutral and irrelevant to virtue
P2Q34.explanation: Aquinas connects moral character to pleasure because the will's goodness is discerned chiefly from the end in which it rests (its pleasure); thus a man's character is revealed by what he takes pleasure in.

P2Q35.q: According to Article 1, to what power do pleasure and pain belong?
options: The intellect alone
The appetite, since both pleasure and pain require conjunction with something under the aspect of good or evil, and good and evil, as such, are objects of the appetite
The five external senses exclusively, with no appetitive component
Neither power; pain and pleasure are purely physiological with no psychological aspect
P2Q35.explanation: Just as pleasure requires conjunction with a good and its perception, pain requires conjunction with an evil and its perception; since good and evil as such are the appetite's objects, both pleasure and pain belong to the appetite.

P2Q35.q: According to Article 6, does Aquinas say sorrow is to be shunned more eagerly than pleasure is to be sought, or vice versa?
options: Sorrow is shunned more eagerly than pleasure is sought, because avoiding evil is naturally the primary motive

Desire for pleasure is naturally more eager than the shunning of sorrow, since a suitable good can be entirely unmixed while an evil is never entirely unsuitable, and good is sought for its own sake while evil is avoided only as a privation
They are always exactly equal in eagerness
Neither pleasure nor sorrow generates any natural eagerness
P2Q35.explanation: Aquinas argues pleasure can be complete and unmixed (a wholly suitable good), while sorrow is always partial (since no evil is wholly unsuitable), and since good is sought for itself while evil is shunned only derivatively, pursuit of pleasure is naturally more eager than avoidance of sorrow.

P2Q35.q: According to Article 2, what distinguishes "sorrow" from mere "pain" in Aquinas's terminology?
options: There is no distinction; the terms are used completely interchangeably in every instance

Sorrow is pain caused specifically by an interior apprehension (of intellect or imagination), while pain caused by exterior sensation alone is called pain but not sorrow, so sorrow is a species of pain
Sorrow refers only to physical injuries, pain only to emotional distress
Sorrow is always more intense than any form of pain
P2Q35.explanation: Since interior apprehension extends to more objects than exterior sense apprehension, Aquinas holds that only pain arising from an interior apprehension is properly called sorrow, making sorrow a species of the broader genus pain.

P2Q36.q: According to Article 1, what does sorrow chiefly regard: the presence of evil or the loss of good?
options: Sorrow can regard either the present evil or the good that is lost, depending on which the appetite's movement chiefly concerns, since even a privation, as apprehended, is regarded as a positive 'contrary'
Sorrow can never regard the loss of a good, only the presence of evil
Sorrow can never regard a present evil, only the loss of a good
There is no meaningful distinction to be made here at all
P2Q36.explanation: Aquinas notes that although evil is really just privation of good, as apprehended by the mind it takes on the character of a positive contrary, so which aspect the movement of sorrow chiefly regards (loss of good or presence of evil) makes a real difference.

P2Q36.q: According to Article 3, does Aquinas connect craving for unity with a cause of sorrow?
options: No, unity and sorrow are entirely unrelated concepts for Aquinas

Yes; since the good of a thing consists in a certain unity, everything naturally desires unity as it desires goodness, so just as love/desire for good causes sorrow (when frustrated), so does craving for unity
Unity is only relevant to metaphysics, never to the passions
Craving for unity is said to be a cause only of pleasure, never of sorrow
P2Q36.explanation: Aquinas links the desire for unity to the desire for good (since a thing's good consists in the unity of its perfecting elements), concluding that craving for unity, like craving for good, can be a cause of sorrow when unfulfilled.

P2Q36.q: According to Article 4, why does Aquinas say an irresistible power is a cause of sorrow?
options: Because being united with a present evil is contrary to the appetite's inclination, and whatever is contrary to a thing's inclination happens to it only through the action of something stronger
Because irresistible power always causes pleasure instead of sorrow
Because power, whether resistible or not, never has any bearing on sorrow
Because irresistible power belongs only to God and thus cannot cause any passion in creatures
P2Q36.explanation: Since union with present evil runs contrary to the appetite's natural inclination, and a thing's inclination is only overridden by something more powerful, Aquinas reasons that a superior, irresistible power is what causes the evil to become present, and hence causes sorrow.

P2Q37.q: According to Article 1, why does pain or sorrow hinder learning?
options: Because all the powers of the soul are rooted in one essence, so when the soul's intention is strongly drawn to one action (dwelling on the painful matter), it is withdrawn from other actions requiring attention, such as learning
Pain has no effect whatsoever on learning or any mental activity
Because pain physically damages the brain in every instance
Because learning requires no attention or intention at all
P2Q37.explanation: Since the soul, being one, has only one intention at a time, if sorrow draws the soul's intention strongly to itself, less remains available for activities like learning that require considerable attention.

P2Q37.q: According to Article 4, why does Aquinas judge sorrow to be more harmful to the body than other passions?
options: Sorrow is not actually more harmful than any other passion

Because sorrow is repugnant to the vital movement of the body specifically in kind (hindering its natural progress), not merely in degree, unlike other passions which may exceed a measure but not oppose the movement's very nature
Because sorrow always causes immediate physical death
Because sorrow is the only passion that has any bodily effect at all
P2Q37.explanation: Aquinas explains that life consists in a certain natural bodily movement; other passions might exceed the due measure of this movement, but sorrow specifically hinders its very progress, making it repugnant to life in kind, not just degree.

P2Q37.q: According to Article 2, how does sorrow "burden" the soul, according to the metaphor Aquinas develops?
options: Sorrow has no metaphorical description in Aquinas's text

Just as fervor is ascribed to love and expansion to pleasure, depression/burdening is ascribed to sorrow because the soul is hindered by a present evil from enjoying what it wishes, similar to being weighed down
Sorrow is described as making the soul lighter and more free
The metaphor of burdening applies only to physical labor, not to sorrow
P2Q37.explanation: Aquinas explains that the soul's passions are named metaphorically from bodily likenesses; sorrow, hindering the will's movement toward what it craves, is likened to being weighed down or depressed by a burden.

P2Q38.q: According to Article 1, does every pleasure assuage sorrow?
options: No pleasure can ever affect sorrow in any way

Yes; since pleasure is a kind of repose of the appetite in a suitable good, and sorrow is a kind of weariness or ailing of the appetite, every pleasure brings relief to sorrow just as bodily repose relieves weariness from any cause
Only pleasures of exactly the same kind as the cause of sorrow can assuage it
Pleasure always increases sorrow rather than relieving it
P2Q38.explanation: Aquinas compares pleasure (repose of appetite) to bodily repose relieving weariness, concluding that any pleasure, regardless of its specific source, can bring some relief to any sorrow.

P2Q38.q: According to Article 3, why does the sympathy of friends assuage sorrow, according to the two reasons Aquinas gives (via Aristotle)?
options: Friends can magically remove the cause of sorrow instantly

First, seeing others share the burden of one's sorrow makes it feel lighter (like sharing a physical load); second, seeing that one is loved by friends who condole gives pleasure, and pleasure assuages sorrow
Friends have no real effect on a person's sorrow at all
Sympathy from friends only works if the friends themselves are not sorrowful
P2Q38.explanation: Aquinas cites Aristotle's twofold explanation: friends sharing our sorrow lessens its felt weight like shared physical burden, and their expressed love gives us pleasure, which in turn assuages sorrow.

P2Q38.q: According to Article 4, does the contemplation of truth assuage pain or sorrow?
options: No, contemplation of truth is entirely unrelated to emotional states

Yes, especially, since the greatest of all pleasures consists in the contemplation of truth, and every pleasure assuages sorrow—illustrated by martyrs who found joy amid physical torment through contemplating divine things
Contemplation of truth only increases sorrow by making one more aware of evils
Only contemplation of purely secular truths has this effect, not divine truths
P2Q38.explanation: Since the greatest pleasure is found in contemplating truth, and every pleasure assuages sorrow, Aquinas concludes contemplation of truth (especially divine truth) is a powerful remedy for sorrow, illustrated by the example of martyrs.

P2Q39.q: According to Article 1, is all sorrow evil?
options: Sorrow is always and only evil, with no qualification whatsoever

Considered simply in itself, sorrow is an evil (an uneasy appetite hindering repose in good); but on the supposition of a present evil, it is a sign of goodness that one is properly saddened by it, since failing to be saddened would itself be evil
Sorrow is always good and never evil in any sense
Sorrow has no moral quality of any kind, being purely physiological
P2Q39.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes sorrow considered absolutely (an evil, since it is an uneasiness of appetite) from sorrow considered relative to a present evil (a sign of goodness, since not grieving at a real evil would itself indicate a defect).

P2Q39.q: According to Article 2, can sorrow be a virtuous good?
options: No, sorrow can never be connected with virtue in any way

Yes; insofar as sorrow denotes right perception of evil (often through right judgment of reason) and rejection of that evil (an act of a well-disposed will), which are the two elements underlying every virtuous good
Sorrow is a virtue only for the Stoics, not for Aquinas
Sorrow is always identical with despair, which cannot be virtuous
P2Q39.explanation: Aquinas argues that perceiving evil correctly and rejecting it through a well-disposed will—the components of interior sorrow—are the same rectitude of reason and will that underlie every virtuous good, so sorrow can be a virtuous good.

P2Q39.q: According to Article 4, is bodily pain the greatest evil a man can suffer?
options: Yes, bodily pain is unequivocally the worst evil possible

No; sorrow or pain for something truly evil is not the greatest evil, since it would be worse not to recognize or reject that evil; and sorrow for an apparent (but really good) evil is not the greatest evil either, since total separation from a true good would be worse
Bodily pain and spiritual pain are always exactly equal in gravity
Pain cannot be evaluated morally at all, according to Aquinas
P2Q39.explanation: Aquinas reasons that whether sorrow concerns a truly evil thing or merely an apparent evil, something worse than the sorrow itself is always conceivable (failing to reject real evil, or being separated from a true good), so no sorrow or pain can be the greatest evil.

P2Q40.q: According to Article 1, how does hope differ from mere desire or cupidity?
options: Hope and desire are entirely identical with no distinction

Hope's object must be good, future, arduous/difficult to obtain, and possible to attain, whereas desire regards the future good absolutely, without requiring difficulty—hope belongs to the irascible faculty, desire to the concupiscible
Desire requires difficulty, but hope does not
Hope concerns only past goods, unlike desire which concerns future goods
P2Q40.explanation: Aquinas identifies four conditions of hope's object: good, future, arduous, and possible; the arduous condition especially distinguishes hope (irascible) from desire/cupidity (concupiscible), which regards future good without requiring difficulty.

P2Q40.q: According to Article 6, why, according to Aquinas, do young men and drunkards tend to be full of hope?
options: Because they have more life experience of failure than others

Because of three reasons tied to hope's object being future, arduous, and possible: youths live much in the future with little past to remember, their heat of nature expands the heart toward the arduous, and inexperience of obstacles makes things seem more possible—drunkards share the causes of heat/high spirits and heedlessness of danger
Because young people and drunkards are inherently more virtuous
Because hope is caused exclusively by wealth, which the young typically possess
P2Q40.explanation: Aquinas, following Aristotle, connects the three conditions of hope's object (future, arduous, possible) to youth's orientation toward the future, natural heat expanding the heart, and inexperience of obstacles—two of which (heat/spirits and heedlessness) also apply to drunkards.

P2Q40.q: According to Article 8, is hope a help or a hindrance to action?
options: Hope always hinders action by making one complacent

Hope is a help to action, both because contemplating something as difficult arouses attention while its possibility does not discourage effort, and because hope causes pleasure, which itself aids action
Hope has no effect whatsoever on action
Hope helps only intellectual actions, never physical ones
P2Q40.explanation: Aquinas explains hope intensifies action both by its object (arduous yet possible, which focuses attention without deterring effort) and by its effect (causing pleasure, which aids action).
